country.comment: Empirical analysis covers Brazilian water supply and sanitation business corporations across all five geographic regions of Brazil.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, and Section 1; PDF p. 4, Section 4

effect_estimate.comment: Note that PDF text extraction omitted minus signs inside Tables 5-7, so coefficient signs are verified directly against the Sections 5.1-5.3 prose (e.g., negative non-significant RRegA and LRegA coefficients in the water model, and negative Psub coefficient in the regulated sanitation/joint models).
effect_estimate.value: In overall GEE models (2005-2012), privately managed corporations charged significantly higher water supply tariffs (+0.3456 R$/m3, p = 0.011, N = 351) and joint water-sanitation tariffs (+0.2797 R$/m3, p = 0.026, N = 351) than publicly managed corporations, while sanitation tariffs alone did not differ significantly (+0.1971 R$/m3, p = 0.159, N = 349). Within regulated corporations (N = 168), private vs. public tariff differences were non-significant (+0.0240 R$/m3, p = 0.885 for water; +0.0647 R$/m3, p = 0.667 jointly), whereas within unregulated corporations (N = 183) private management increased water and joint tariffs by +0.3618 R$/m3 (p = 0.011) and sanitation tariffs by +0.2906 R$/m3 (p = 0.095, N = 182). Neither regional/state regulatory agencies (RRegA: -0.0482 R$/m3, p = 0.656 for water; p = 0.959 jointly) nor local/municipal regulatory agencies (LRegA: -0.0774 R$/m3, p = 0.580 for water; -0.0889 R$/m3, p = 0.560 jointly) achieved significantly lower tariffs than unregulated utilities, and neither rate-of-return (Rrat: +0.1558 R$/m3, p = 0.244 for water; +0.1698 R$/m3, p = 0.191 jointly) nor price-cap/revenue-cap regimes (Rcap: +0.1204 R$/m3, p = 0.404 for water; +0.0397 R$/m3, p = 0.786 jointly) yielded lower tariffs than municipally negotiated tariffs (within regulated utilities, rate-of-return increased water tariffs by +0.3080 R$/m3, p = 0.015 and joint tariffs by +0.2701 R$/m3, p = 0.032). Increasing block tariffs were associated with higher joint tariffs than two-part uniform volumetric tariffs (TwoIBT: +0.3726 R$/m3, p = 0.010; SinIBT: +0.3115 R$/m3, p = 0.029).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 7-10, Sections 5.1-5.3; PDF pp. 8-9, Tables 5, 6, and 7

mechanism_certainty.comment: Documented statistical association (level 1) between utility governance/regulatory variables and average billed tariff levels in observational panel GEE regressions; design ceiling prevents >= 3, and administrative tariff-setting or household-level processes are not directly observed empirically.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines water and sanitation tariff levels, block vs. uniform volumetric tariff structures, and government capital subsidies (BURDEN: fees); laxity/discretion in unregulated municipal tariff negotiation vs. formal rate-of-return and price/revenue-cap regimes (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion; ENFORCEMENT); regulatory tariff discounts/sanctions for water and sewage quality non-compliance (ENFORCEMENT: sanction); and decentralized municipal vs. state/micro-regional regulatory agencies and multi-municipal concessions (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination). Social tariffs are mentioned as background but explicitly excluded from empirical scope on PDF p. 11.
mechanism_flags.value: BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, fees, discretion, sanction, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 2-3, Sections 2.1-2.2; PDF pp. 4-6, Section 4.1; PDF pp. 10-11, Section 5.4 and Appendix 1

outcome_flags.comment: Dependent variables are utility-level average billed water supply, sanitation, and joint tariff levels in R$/m3 (consumer price/tariff levels framed around cost recovery vs. equity and universal access). Water quality compliance (coliforms, chlorine, turbidity) and sewage treatment indices are included as explanatory covariates rather than outcomes.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Observational longitudinal panel study following 51 corporations over 2005-2012 using GEE regression (independent working correlation matrix) comparing existing ownership and regulatory structures without a quasi-experimental intervention comparator (no DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, or policy panel fixed-effects design).

sample_size.comment: Of 52 Brazilian water and sanitation business corporations (22 private companies and 30 public-controlled mixed capital companies), 1 lacked available data, yielding an unbalanced panel of 51 corporations from 2005 to 2012; 2 outlier corporation-year observations (COSANPA in 2007 and 2011) were excluded from the sanitation tariff model.
sample_size.value: 51 water and sanitation business corporations; 351 corporation-year observations (2005-2012) for water supply and joint tariff models (168 regulated, 183 unregulated) and 349 corporation-year observations for the sanitation tariff model (167 regulated, 182 unregulated)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 4, Section 4; PDF p. 7, Section 4.2; PDF pp. 8-9, Tables 4-7

study_design.comment: Unbalanced 8-year panel (2005-2012) of 51 corporations analyzed via Gaussian identity-link Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) with an independent working correlation matrix and robust standard errors across overall, regulated, and unregulated subsamples.
study_design.value: Longitudinal unbalanced panel observational study (2005-2012) using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) regression
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 4, Section 4; PDF pp. 6-7, Section 4.2
